British Journal of Educational Technolog.title: From emotion regulation to academic success: A self‐determination theory‐based emotional agent‐mediated approach
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    Emotion regulation has been recognized as a key factor affecting students' academic success. However, in conventional school settings, it is challenging to foster students' emotion regulation owing to the involvement of complex factors that might influence students' conscious and unconscious behaviours. To address this issue, a self‐determination theory (SDT)‐based emotional agent framework was proposed, and an emotional agent (EmoAgent), capable of proactively detecting students' emotional states and providing emotional regulation strategies to individual students in addition to the provision of conventional learning supports, was implemented. To assess the effectiveness of the proposed approach, an 8‐week quasi‐experiment was designed with 173 sixth graders from four classes taking the Information Technology course in a primary school. Two classes (87 students) comprised the experimental group (EG) which used the SDT‐based emotional agent‐mediated (SDT‐EA) approach, while the other two classes (86 students) comprised the control group (CG) which learned with the SDT‐based conventional agent (STD‐CA), which is capable of providing learning supports but without considering emotional factors. The experimental results showed that (1) the SDT‐EA approach significantly outperformed the SDT‐CA approach in academic achievement; (2) the SDT‐EA approach engaged students in positive emotional experiences, whereas the SDT‐CA approach exposed students to more negative emotional experiences; (3) negative emotion was significantly negatively associated with academic achievement, moderated by the SDT‐EA approach.
                  
                  
                    
                    
                      
                        
                          Practitioner notes
                        
                        
                          What is already known about this topic?
                          
                            
                              Within self‐determination theory, if the three psychological needs of autonomy, competence and relatedness are met, students’ intrinsic motivation is activated and in turn their academic emotion is regulated, which shapes their well‐being, engagement and academic success.
                            
                            
                              GenAI–human collaboration can facilitate students’ self‐determined and personalized learning.
                            
                            
                              Most pedagogical agents tend to assist with personalized cognitive support rather than with emotion regulation or emotional support.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          What does this paper add?
                          
                            
                              Merging affective computing technology with GenAI, this study constructed an emotional agent with emotion sensing, recognition, feedback and regulation, providing emotional and cognitive supports.
                            
                            
                              Using process mining techniques, this study found that the emotional agent facilitated students’ emotion regulation from negative to positive.
                            
                            
                              The emotional agent moderated the effect of negative emotions on academic success.
                            
                            
                              The emotional agent can significantly promote academic achievement.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          Implications for practice and/or policy
                          
                            
                              The study findings imply that the SDT‐based emotional agent‐mediated approach shows promise for strengthening students’ self‐regulated learning.
                            
                            
                              The study offers a viable model for integrating socio‐emotional learning with subject‐matter instruction.
                            
                            
                              The SDT‐based emotional agent can be embedded in regular instruction to instantiate a self‐determined learning paradigm.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title:
Effects of
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    chatbot‐supported cooperative flipped classroom on student collaboration, self‐regulated learning and academic performance: A mastery learning perspective
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    Despite the increasing application of AI chatbots, few studies have examined the effectiveness of AI chatbot‐supported cooperative‐flipped classrooms in university teaching. Based on mastery learning theory, this study employed a quasi‑experimental design to examine how an AI chatbot‐supported cooperative‑flipped classroom influences students' collaboration, self‐regulated learning and academic performance, and whether students with different prior knowledge levels demonstrate distinct patterns under AI‐supported flipped learning. This study involved 154 junior students from a normal university, including an experimental group (
                    n
                     = 87) and a control group (
                    n
                     = 67), who were taught by the same instructor over an 11‐week period. Quantitative data from pretest and posttest scores and self‑report scales were analysed using
                    t
                    ‐tests and ANCOVA, whereas qualitative interview data from 10 experimental group students were analysed using Epistemic Network Analysis to compare collaboration and self‑regulated learning patterns across prior knowledge groups. The results showed that, compared to the control group, the experimental group demonstrated significantly higher posttest scores in collaboration, self‐regulated learning and academic performance. Within the experimental group, students with higher levels of AI chatbot interaction also significantly outperformed those with lower interaction levels in academic performance. Further, Epistemic Network Analysis results revealed that in AI chatbot‑supported flipped learning, students with lower prior knowledge exhibited denser collaboration networks, requiring more cognitive input and more frequent dimension switching to coordinate collaborative processes. In contrast, students with higher prior knowledge demonstrated stronger connections between the seeking, engaging and reflecting dimensions in their self‐regulated learning networks, reflecting more integrated self‐regulatory behaviour. This study provides empirical support for mastery learning theory and demonstrates the effectiveness of AI chatbot‐supported cooperative‐flipped classrooms, offering implications for differentiated teaching based on students' prior knowledge levels.
                  
                  
                    
                      
                        Practitioner notes
                      
                      
                        What is already known about this topic
                        
                          
                            
                              Flipped classrooms are associated with improvements in students' self‐regulated learning, motivation and academic performance compared with traditional instruction.
                            
                            
                              Group cooperation during pre‐class activities can enhance peer interaction and collaboration, but is often constrained by uneven participation and limited instructional support.
                            
                            
                              AI chatbots have been applied as learning assistants in higher education to provide feedback and learning resources, yet their role in structured pre‐class group cooperation remains insufficiently examined.
                            
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        What this paper adds
                        
                          
                            
                              AI chatbot‐supported cooperative‐flipped classrooms significantly enhance students' collaboration, self‐regulated learning and academic performance compared with traditional group‐based flipped learning.
                            
                            
                              Epistemic network analysis shows that students with different levels of prior knowledge exhibit distinct collaboration and self‐regulation patterns when supported by an AI chatbot.
                            
                            
                              The findings demonstrate that AI chatbots can function as mastery‐oriented scaffolds by guiding task division, clarifying learning goals and supporting feedback during pre‐class group discussions, thereby strengthening students' readiness for subsequent in‐class learning.
                            
                          
                        
                      
                      
                        Implications for practice and/or policy
                        
                          
                            
                              Practitioners are encouraged to integrate AI chatbots into pre‐class group discussions to provide structured guidance, timely feedback and support for collaborative knowledge construction.
                            
                            
                              Instructional support should be differentiated by prior knowledge: learners with lower prior knowledge benefit from clearer goals and stronger cognitive scaffolding, whereas higher‐achieving learners benefit from tasks emphasizing integration, reflection and assessment.
                            
                            
                              For large‐scale or resource‐constrained teaching contexts, AI chatbot‐supported cooperative‐flipped classrooms offer a scalable approach to implementing mastery learning and differentiated instruction in technology‐enhanced pedagogy.

British Journal of Educational Technolog.title: Not all collaboration benefits from competition: Collaboration modes in a computational thinking game
British Journal of Educational Technolog.abstract:
Abstract
                  
                    
                    Digital game‐based learning often leverages social dynamics to enhance engagement, yet the interplay between collaborative structures and competitive pressures remains complex. This study investigated different collaboration modes and how they interact with competition to influence computational thinking (CT) learning, group metacognition and in‐game behaviours. Adopting a quasi‐experimental approach with a 3 × 2 factorial design, 148 seventh‐grade students were recruited via purposive sampling from intact classes. Participants played the game in pairs, with or without competition, in one of three collaboration modes: paired gaming on one computer, collaboration on respective computers with turn‐taking or cooperation on respective computers with role assignment. Data were analysed using quantitative methods to assess learning outcomes and behavioural sequence analysis to identify interaction patterns. Results revealed significant main effects of collaboration mode and an interaction effect between collaboration and competition. The cooperative group with competition achieved the highest CT outcomes, and the paired gaming group with competition reported the highest level of group metacognition. In contrast, the collaborative group with competition had the lowest level of learning outcomes and group metacognition. Behavioural sequence analyses identified unique patterns that corroborate the quantitative findings. Notably, competition undermined the collaborative turn‐taking mode while enhancing cooperative and paired gaming modes, highlighting the need to carefully match collaboration structures with competitive elements in designing game‐based learning.
                  
                  
                    
                    
                      
                        
                          Practitioner notes
                        
                        
                          What is already known about this topic
                          
                            
                              Collaboration and competition are widely used in digital game‐based learning (DGBL) to enhance engagement, motivation and problem‐solving.
                            
                            
                              Prior studies have often examined collaboration and competition separately, leaving the interactive effects between these social dynamics on computational thinking (CT) and group metacognition underexplored.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          What this paper adds
                          
                            
                              Different collaboration modes significantly shaped CT learning and group metacognition.
                            
                            
                              Competition alone showed no benefits for CT learning or group metacognition.
                            
                            
                              Cooperative + competition fostered clear roles, strategic play and higher CT.
                            
                            
                              Competition weakened collaboration learning's CT performance and led to fragmented behaviours.
                            
                          
                        
                        
                          Implications for practice and policy
                          
                            
                              Carefully match collaboration structures with competition features when designing game‐based or group learning activities.
                            
                            
                              Use competition selectively—beneficial in cooperative tasks with clear role assignments, but potentially detrimental in open collaboration requiring trust and mutual regulation.
                            
                            
                              Integrate competitive and collaborative elements intentionally rather than additively.

Educational Technology Research and Deve.title: Academics’ (Re) construction of teacher identities in the context of technology integration at a South African university
Educational Technology Research and Deve.abstract:
Abstract
                  Integrating technology into higher education teaching is reshaping pedagogical practices and prompting academics to (re)construct their professional identities. This qualitative case study explores how academics at a South African university respond to these changes, drawing on identity theory and the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) model to analyse the data. Data were collected from 12 purposively selected academics through semi-structured interviews and were analysed thematically. Findings indicate that academics are compelled to transition from traditional to interactive, student-centred teaching, requiring ongoing adaptation to emerging digital tools, multimedia integration, and data analytics for student monitoring. However, this shift also introduced identity tensions driven by increased workload, student disengagement, and recurring technical issues. Despite these challenges, the participants reported enhanced pedagogical effectiveness and renewed engagement through digital methods. The study highlights the dual nature of technology integration as both a disruptor and an enabler of professional growth and argues for comprehensive institutional support structures, including professional development and technical assistance. The findings contribute to the discourse on teacher identity in digitally evolving higher education environments and offer practical implications for policies and professional learning.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title: Learning Dynamics in Asynchronous Online Higher Education: Instructional Design, Self‐Regulated Learning Supports, and Academic Performance
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Online learning has become a defining feature of higher education, expanding access while reshaping how students engage with knowledge, instructors, and peers. Despite its rapid growth, uncertainty persists regarding which instructional design features most effectively support academic achievement and digital competence in asynchronous, skills‐based courses. Prior studies often focus on perceptions or rely on small cross‐sectional samples, leaving limited clarity on how specific design features such as assignments, badges, and feedback influence measurable academic outcomes in asynchronous, skills‐based courses.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This study examines how assignment structures, learning supports, pacing systems, and digital badges are associated with standardized academic performance in an asynchronous pre‐finance computer applications course, drawing on the community of inquiry framework (CoI) and self‐regulated learning (SRL) theory to interpret how instructional design features and regulatory processes interact to shape academic outcomes.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    
                      Data were collected from 742 undergraduates across six consecutive semesters in a certified asynchronous online course emphasizing Microsoft Excel proficiency. Survey responses on learning materials (e.g.,
                      SimuTraining
                      ,
                      CapstoneProjects
                      ) and instructional supports (e.g.,
                      WeeklyUpdates
                      ,
                      QuizFeedback
                      ) were matched with performance records (i.e.,
                      Points
                      : total points earned), which were standardized using
                      z
                      ‐scores (
                      ZTP
                      ) to ensure comparability across semesters while preserving students' relative standing within each term. A pooled regression with semester fixed effects and robust standard errors examined factors associated with performance while controlling cohort and seasonal differences.
                    
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    Earning a digital badge, resubmitting capstone projects, and receiving automated feedback were positively linked to performance, while valuing unlimited attempts on low‐stakes assignments and preferring end‐of‐course deadlines were negatively associated. These results reveal a disconnect between student perceptions and actual learning, suggesting that lower‐performing students may rely on repetition without mastering underlying skills. Findings underscore the importance of structured pacing, targeted feedback, and performance‐linked incentives such as badges. Collectively, this study advances technology‐enhanced education by clarifying which practices foster success and offering strategies to strengthen digital competence and learning outcomes in higher education.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title: The Complexity of Visual Learning Materials Moderates the Effects of Instructors' Facial Expressions in Instructional Videos
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Research shows that instructors' happy facial expressions can evoke students' positive emotions and enhance their learning motivation. Nevertheless, debate persists in the literature regarding the impact of instructors' happy facial expressions on students' learning performance. This may be attributed to the potential social benefits of instructors' happy facial expressions being counterbalanced by the concurrent attentional costs.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This study examined whether the visual complexity of learning materials (simple vs. complex) moderated the effect of instructors' facial expressions (happy vs. bored) on students' learning performance.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    
                      Participants (
                      n
                       = 58) watched two instructional videos featuring an instructor displaying either happy or bored facial expressions while presenting either complex or simple visual materials.
                    
                  
                  
                    Result and Conclusions
                    The experimental results revealed that, when simple visual learning materials were used, the instructor's happy facial expressions significantly improved students' learning performance. In contrast, when complex visual learning materials were used, differences in the instructor's facial expressions did not significantly affect students' learning performance.
                  
                  
                    Implications
                    Our findings suggest that instructors should consider both the complexity of the visual learning materials and their facial expressions when teaching English vocabulary as a foreign language through instructional videos, particularly when teaching female students. Specifically, when using simple visual learning materials, instructors should display happy facial expressions to enhance student performance. Conversely, when using complex visual learning materials, instructors should avoid overly expressive facial expressions that may distract students from the learning content.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title: Virtual Reality and Augmented Reality Technology for Safety Training in High‐Risk Environments: A Systematic Literature Review on Perspectives and Challenges
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Effective safety training in high‐risk industries including construction, mining, manufacturing, aviation and nuclear energy is critically important, as inadequate hazard awareness and human error consistently contribute to occupational fatalities and severe incidents.
                  
                  
                    Method
                    This systematic review synthesises evidence from 66 studies published between 2015 and 2026 across 29 countries to evaluate the application and effectiveness of virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) technologies for safety training in these sectors. A comprehensive literature search was conducted across Scopus and Web of Science.
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    The findings show that VR demonstrates consistent effectiveness for deep skill acquisition and hazard recognition through high‐fidelity simulation of environments too dangerous for real‐world practice, evidenced by its universal adoption in mining and predominant use in nuclear emergency training. AR provides complementary value for situated learning and just‐in‐time performance support, enhancing procedural accuracy and situational awareness in construction, manufacturing and railway contexts. Extended reality (XR) configurations facilitate collaborative training for dynamic risk scenarios requiring integration of real and simulated elements. Sector‐specific adoption patterns reflect strategic alignment between technological affordances and industrial priorities, with aviation exhibiting the most sophisticated behavioural assessment frameworks. However, critical gaps constrain the evidence base: longitudinal assessments examining knowledge retention beyond immediate post‐training remain exceptionally rare; the predominance of student samples limits ecological validity; assessment beyond Kirkpatrick Level 2 (learning) is exceptional; and the absence of standardised competency metrics hinders cross‐study synthesis. This review concludes that immersive technologies represent promising complementary tools for safety training, offering distinctive pedagogical affordances that address limitations of conventional methods.

Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.title: The Disfluency Effect Revisited: Why Audiovisual Channel Manipulations Impair Motivation and Trigger Illusions Without Boosting Learning
Journal of Computer Assisted Learning.abstract:
ABSTRACT
                  
                    Background
                    Previous research on multimedia learning has predominantly applied perceptual disfluency consistently across both visual and auditory channels within instructional materials. Such dual‐channel disfluency may impose excessive extraneous cognitive load (ECL), thereby undermining learning outcomes. The disfluency effect, however, posits that perceptual disruptions to processing fluency can, under specific conditions, facilitate learning. Nevertheless, empirical evidence regarding the efficacy of disfluency manipulations in audiovisual learning environments remains inconclusive.
                  
                  
                    Objectives
                    This study investigated whether a more nuanced application of disfluency, as a means of cognitive load manipulation, can yield positive effects in video‐based learning. Specifically, we examined how progressively reducing ECL through controlled disfluency manipulations influences learning performance, metacognitive judgements (judgements of learning), learning motivation and subjective learning experiences.
                  
                  
                    Methods
                    
                      Experiment 1 examined the effects of varying degrees of disfluency in audiovisual channels (fully fluent, partially disfluent, fully disfluent) on multimedia learning outcomes (
                      n
                       = 48). Experiment 2 built upon these materials by further attempting to mitigate ECL through the separation of visual and auditory disfluent information. It employed a 2 (channel: visual channel; auditory channel) × 2 (fluency: partially disfluent; fully disfluent) between‐subjects design (
                      n
                       = 109).
                    
                  
                  
                    Results and Conclusions
                    Results from Experiment 1 indicated that, although disfluency manipulations in audiovisual channels increased ECL, they reduced learning motivation and induced metacognitive overestimation, while having no significant effect on learning performance. In Experiment 2, all four experimental groups showed significantly higher ECL than the fully fluent dual‐channel group, whereas learning performance remained unaffected. Disfluency also led to metacognitive overestimation and a significant decrease in learning motivation across conditions. Overall, these findings do not support the disfluency effect in video‐based learning. Rather than enhancing learning performance, disfluency was associated with inflated metacognitive judgements (illusions) and reduced learner motivation.

Education and Information Technologies.title: Extending the theory of planned behaviour to explain contract cheating in the age of generative AI: evidence from Australian higher education
Education and Information Technologies.abstract:
Abstract
                  Academic contract cheating (CC) poses a significant challenge for Higher Education (HE), a problem that has become more complex with the increasing use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (Gen AI) tools. While similarity detection software can flag AI-generated text, it remains ineffective in identifying CC, potentially displacing misconduct rather than reducing it. Drawing on and extending the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB), this study examines how traditional TPB constructs and technology-mediated perceptual factors jointly influence students’ intentions and behaviours related to CC within the Australian HE context. The findings reveal significant direct and indirect pathways linking perceived instructor involvement, detection awareness, AI-related risk perceptions, and perceived behavioural control to students’ intentions and behaviours. These results extend the TPB framework to the context of AI-mediated academic misconduct and offer practical implications for universities in Australia and potentially other similar contexts. The study provides actionable insights for HE institutions to design integrity policies, assessment strategies, detection mechanisms, and digital literacy initiatives to strengthen academic integrity in alignment with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) on Quality Education (Goal 4).

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Measuring Secondary School Students’ Verification Capability in GenAI-Supported Learning: Development and Application of the α − v − M Framework
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) provides adolescents with fluent and immediate support, but unverified use may encourage cognitive offloading and passive reliance. This study conceptualizes verification capability as a cognitive defense mechanism through which learners inspect, question, correct, compare, or reconstruct GenAI outputs before accepting them. Using an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design, we first conducted deductive qualitative coding of 762 authentic Human–AI collaborative teaching cases. Among 242 valid GenAI-supported cases, 98.8% showed no documented verification of AI-generated outputs, indicating a severe observable verification deficit. We then developed and validated the
                    
                      
                        
                          α
                          −
                          v
                          −
                          M
                        
                      
                    
                    framework, comprising AI Engagement, Verification Intensity, and Multi-model Cross-validation, through a scale study with 422 secondary school students. Psychometric validation provided generally supportive evidence for the scale structure, and Item Response Theory was used to evaluate item functioning and generate latent trait scores. Structural equation modeling showed that AI engagement was associated with human–AI collaborative quality through verification-related processes. Gaussian graphical modeling identified deep logical auditing as a central cognitive defense indicator. Latent profile analysis further revealed four learner profiles: Naïve Trusters, Superficial Checkers, Isolated Auditors, and Symbiotic Strategists. These findings inform GenAI-supported learning design by emphasizing cognitive friction, verification scaffolds, and profile-sensitive feedback.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: The Impact of Generative AI on Self-Efficacy: Evidence From a Meta-Analysis
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (genAI) tools such as ChatGPT are increasingly used in education. While many studies have examined how genAI tools affect learning, we know less about how genAI tools influence motivational factors such as learners’ self-efficacy, despite the central role self-efficacy plays in motivation and learning. We conducted a meta-analysis of experimental and quasi-experimental research to examine the effect of genAI tools on learners’ self-efficacy. Studies published between November 2022 and February 2026 were systematically searched and screened, yielding 84 independent effects in our analysis. The results showed that using genAI during learning improved learners’ self-efficacy with a moderate effect size. However, the size of this effect depended on how genAI was used. Implementations where genAI acted as a tutor that guided students’ learning produced larger improvements in self-efficacy than uses where AI only (1) provided feedback, (2) answered questions, or (3) replaced learner work. Also, longer interventions produced stronger improvements than brief interactions. The improvements in self-efficacy did not differ across academic domains or learner age groups. These findings suggest that genAI can support learners’ self-efficacy when it is used to scaffold learning and encourage active engagement. The results highlight the importance of how genAI is integrated into instruction when designing AI-supported learning environments.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Fostering Pre-Service Teachers’ Professional Problem Solving and Higher-Order Thinking Skills With a GenAI-Powered Interactive Fiction-Based Adaptive Teaching Simulation
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence offers substantial potential for teacher education programs; however, its passive or uncritical use may undermine higher-order thinking skills. Despite growing interest, empirical evidence on how GenAI can be pedagogically designed to actively foster professional cognition in pre-service teachers remains limited. Addressing this gap, the present study investigates the effects of a GenAI-powered Interactive Fiction–based Adaptive Teaching Simulation on pre-service teachers’ professional problem-solving skills and higher-order thinking skills. Using a sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, the present study involved 114 pre-service teachers, comprising a treatment group that engaged with the simulation and a control group that received non-simulation-based instruction. After controlling for pre-test scores, the treatment group obtained significantly higher post-test scores than the control group on the thinking and evaluator subdimensions of professional problem solving. Additionally, the treatment group showed higher adjusted post-test critical thinking scores than the control group, with a medium effect size. The qualitative findings supported these results, revealing that the system fostered reflective decision-making, multi-perspective reasoning, professional preparedness, and more informed and cautious perceptions regarding the use of GenAI in educational contexts. Overall, this study provides practical and theoretical implications for the pedagogically grounded integration of GenAI-powered Interactive Fiction simulations into teacher education programs.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: A Peer Assessment-Based Metaverse Inquiry Task Approach to Promoting Learning Achievement, Critical Thinking, Collaboration, and Creative Thinking: Evidence From Statistical and Epistemic Network Analysis
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract:
The metaverse provides new opportunities for designing learning activities in Information Systems (IS) education. This study integrated a pedagogical approach with the metaverse and examined its effectiveness on learning achievement, critical thinking awareness, collaborative tendencies, and creative thinking skills. A total of 50 university students (
                    M
                    
                      age
                    
                    =
                    19.4 years) participated in this quasi-experimental study. The experimental group engaged in a peer-assessment-based metaverse AICDR (Asking, Investigating, Creating, Discussing, and Reflecting) inquiry task (PA-MIT), while the control group followed a conventional metaverse AICDR inquiry task (C-MIT) over an 11-week intervention. Data were analyzed using ANCOVA to compare group differences in learning achievement, critical thinking awareness, and collaboration tendency, while epistemic network analysis (ENA) was applied to explore creative thinking patterns. Results showed that the PA-MIT group achieved significantly higher learning achievement and greater critical thinking awareness than the C-MIT group. However, no significant difference was found in collaboration tendencies. ENA further revealed stronger links among originality, flexibility, and fluency in the PA-MIT group, while the C-MIT group demonstrated strengths in elaboration, flexibility, and fluency. Results highlighted the role of the PA-MIT approach in fostering originality-oriented creative thinking. Peer feedback and idea exchange may lead to the interconnectedness of higher frequency originality-related discourse.

Journal of Educational Computing Researc.title: Differentiated Formative Feedback Through Parameterized ChatGPT: Effects on Knowledge Construction, Engagement, and Higher-Order Thinking in STEM Education
Journal of Educational Computing Researc.abstract: STEM education increasingly emphasizes interdisciplinary integration and self-directed learning, yet students with different achievement levels often face unequal challenges when navigating complex cross-domain content. High-achieving students may lack sufficient cognitive stimulation, whereas low-achieving students may struggle with overwhelming complexity. Standard ChatGPT feedback lacks adaptability to these diverse learner capabilities, leaving some students unchallenged and others overloaded. Addressing these disparities requires timely and differentiated instructional support. This study proposes AdjustGPT, a system that calibrates ChatGPT’s generative parameters (temperature, max_tokens, frequency_penalty, presence_penalty, and top_p) according to learners’ achievement levels to deliver differentiated formative feedback. Grounded in formative feedback theory and cognitive load principles, AdjustGPT provides high-achieving students with exploratory, multi-perspective feedback that fosters critical thinking and innovation, while offering low-achieving students clear, structured guidance that reduces cognitive load and strengthens foundational understanding. A quasi-experimental study with 62 university students in a STEM course showed that, within this exploratory sample, AdjustGPT was associated with significant gains in knowledge construction, cognitive and emotional engagement, and higher-order thinking outcomes, including critical thinking and problem-solving. These findings provide initial evidence that parameterized ChatGPT systems can support adaptive formative feedback and differentiated AI-assisted teaching in STEM education. Larger-scale studies are needed to establish robustness and generalizability.

Early Childhood Education Journal.title: School Readiness and Home Visiting: A Scoping Review of Definitions, Outcomes, and Contextual Moderators
Early Childhood Education Journal.abstract:
Abstract
                  This scoping review examined empirical research on the relationship between participation in home visiting programs and children’s school readiness at the time of school entry. Specifically, we explored how school readiness is defined across studies, which domains are assessed as outcomes, and what contextual factors moderate the effects of home visiting on school readiness. School readiness is a multidimensional construct encompassing physical well-being, social-emotional development, language and literacy, approaches to learning, and cognitive skills. Home visiting programs aim to promote early development and family well-being, yet evidence remains mixed regarding their impact on school readiness and the contextual factors that shape these outcomes. This review addresses these gaps by mapping the scope and characteristics of existing research. A systematic search of CINAHL Plus, Embase, PubMed, and Scopus was conducted for articles published between January 2016 and April 2025. Guided by PRISMA-ScR, studies were included if they examined U.S. based- home visiting or home-based interventions for children from birth through kindergarten and assessed school readiness at school entry. Twenty studies met inclusion criteria. Definitions of school readiness and the developmental domains assessed varied widely across studies, with language and literacy and social emotional development most frequently examined. Evidence of home visiting effectiveness was mixed but generally indicated positive impacts on child language, social emotional development, and early cognitive skills. Five studies identified contextual moderators of program effectiveness, including parent academic expectations, program language, child sex and temperament, implementation fidelity, and home visiting intensity. These moderators shaped the strength of intervention effects on school readiness outcomes. Findings indicate that while home visiting programs can strengthen key domains of early development, variation in the definition of school readiness limits comparability across studies. Contextual moderators at the individual and program levels emerged as important drivers of effectiveness, yet no studies assessed community or structural-level factors despite their known influence on school readiness. These gaps highlight the need for a shared conceptual model of school readiness and for research that incorporates broader ecological contexts to better understand how home visiting achieves its impacts. Overall, home visiting programs show potential to strengthen key domains of early development, but inconsistent definitions and measures of school readiness limit comparability across studies. The evidence base centers largely on individual and program-level moderators, leaving broader ecological and structural influences unexamined. Future research should adopt shared readiness frameworks and incorporate multilevel contextual factors to more fully understand how home visiting contributes to school readiness.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Reimagining Froebelian principles to engage and support low-income families in early childhood policy
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: This paper makes three important contributions to the early years field in England. First, it highlights the barriers to play experienced by low-income families. Second, it illuminates parents’ affinity with Froebelian principles without prior knowledge of them. Third, it suggests how these affinities could be taken up in early years policy. This paper draws on previous research which revealed that many early years’ practitioners believe low-income families often do not value play. In so doing, it presents findings from our recent study which invited low-income families to reflect on and explore the potential of applying Froebel’s ideas in their interactions with their child(ren) during play. Through interviews, families shared their experiences, perceptions, and understandings of Froebelian approaches to play. Notably, parents engaged with Froebelian concepts in practice, even though they did not explicitly identify or label them as such. The findings suggest a need to adapt and extend Froebelian principles to be more inclusive and accessible to low-income families. This research offers valuable insights for practitioners by providing empirical evidence of diverse parental perspectives on play, highlighting opportunities to learn from families and support play-based learning at home. It also holds implications for policy, identifying areas where changes are needed to address the impact of socio-economic disadvantage on families with young children.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Organizational culture in leading pedagogical work in Finnish early childhood education: A discourse analysis
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Finnish early childhood education has undergone many changes over the past decade. These changes have strengthened the position of Early Childhood Education (ECE) within the education system. ECE teachers are now responsible for planning the activities for groups of children, implementation of activities with a goal-oriented and systematic approach and evaluating and developing the activities. ECE teachers are responsible for leading the pedagogical activities of the multiprofessional team; however the leadership role of teachers remains unclear. This study examines how organizational culture is constructed in discourses on leading pedagogical work in Finnish ECE. The theoretical framework is based on the concepts of pedagogical leadership, distributed pedagogical leadership, teacher leadership, and organizational culture. The data consist of interviews with 11 ECE teachers. We analysed the data using discourse analysis as a method. We identified four discourses in the data: the discourse of varied clarity, the discourse of balancing act, the discourse of competition, and the discourse of varied support. Considering this study, there are varying organizational cultural prerequisites for leading a team’s pedagogical activities in Finnish ECE. The results can help to understand the phenomenon of teacher leadership. The results can also help centre directors develop the organization’s culture so that it better supports teachers in their leadership task.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Educators’ perspectives on early language facilitation with children aged birth to 2 years in early childhood education and care in Finland
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: The first two years of life are critical for later language learning and performance. With an increasing number of children participating in institutional early childhood education and care (ECEC), this has become an important language learning environment. ECEC educators play a key role in facilitating children’s language development and hence their views on the possibilities and constraints for facilitating young children’s language in ECEC are valuable. The study presented in this paper, explored educators’ views on aspects linked to early language facilitation in ECEC with children aged birth to two years. A large-scale semi-structured survey related to early language facilitation in ECEC was completed by 644 educators. Their open-ended responses were analysed using qualitative inductive content analysis. Factors constraining and facilitating language development in ECEC were extracted from the data and grouped into four categories: characteristics of educators as prerequisites for language facilitation; daily group practices in ECEC; ECEC service policy and resources; and ECEC in the context of wider societal and family services. While many existing well-functioning practices for early language facilitation were noted, challenges were also reported. In addition to employing skilled staff, educators saw it as important to organise practices and daily routines in ways that support language facilitation. They also emphasised that setting lower educator-child ratios and taking children’s skills and age into account when forming groups would create more frequent language-facilitation situations involving educator-child reciprocal communications. Overall, the educators perceived ECEC as a low-threshold service for early language intervention. They considered language facilitation for young children to be essential and to require multi-professional cooperation and resources.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: “I like to play with my Grandfriends”: Participants’ experiences in a co-located intergenerational program
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: Research on intergenerational programs (IGPs) has documented cognitive, physical and social outcomes for older adults, and beneficial effects for children such as enhanced empathy and more positive attitudes toward older adults. However, there is a relative scarcity of research documenting the benefits of co-located intergenerational programs, whereby the aged-care facility and early learning program are housed under the same roof, thus offering opportunities for frequent intergenerational connections across structured and unstructured activities. Moreover, research providing a consolidated account of the benefits of participation from the perspectives of multiple participant groups, especially young children, is limited. As such, this qualitative case study explores the perspectives of multiple participants engaged in a co-located aged-care facility and early learning centre in Melbourne, Australia: 19 young children and their families, seven early learning and aged-care staff, and seven older adults. The methodology involved semi-structured interviews conducted with staff, online surveys completed by families, and draw, write, and tell method to elicit children’s perspectives. The analysis was framed by social capital theory which pays attention to the relationships within and between groups (bonding and bridging), and the associated benefits for individual and group capabilities. Thematic analysis of the qualitative data revealed two overarching themes – “Program design and implementation” and “Impact for participants” – comprising five categories which highlight the importance of relational factors to nurture mutually beneficial bridging and bonding relationships, and structural program elements such as collaborative planning to support optimal outcomes for all participants.

Journal of Early Childhood Research.title: Children’s use of symbolic “anchors”: Color and shape in map-making activities
Journal of Early Childhood Research.abstract: This research study focuses on children’s symbolic development, especially looking at color and shape as symbolic anchors in children’s expressive communication. Framed by Vygotsky’s cognitive development theory, which includes the roles of social interaction, cultural tools, and the zone of proximal development (ZPD), as well as Mead’s social interactionism, the study was designed as mixed-methods research with data collection from children’s map artifacts, map-making video recording and audio transcriptions, and a data collection matrix. By tracking the performance of 10 children (n/x = 10) in creating maps for 2 years, when they were approximately 4 years old (year 1, mean age = 52.5 months), and in Pre-K (year 2, mean age = 71 months), when they were approximately 5 years old, we examined children’s symbol use. It was observed that exposure to and engagement with relational language promotes children’s analogical reasoning. We also found that the children’s use of symbols, and especially symbolic anchors, increased overtime, demonstrating expanded perspective-taking ability. Lastly, it is our observation that children’s use of shape as a symbolic anchor seems to appear prior to children’s use of color in the emergence of symbolic representation.

keyword_papers.title: Applying Artificial Intelligence into Early Childhood Math Education: Lesson Design and Course Effect
keyword_papers.abstract: A growing trend has been observed in applying artificial intelligence (Al) for educational purposes. With emerging initiatives in adapting Al in early childhood education, greater effort can be made in providing empirical evidence to theoretically support the use of Al techniques for young children. This study aims to introduce an instructional unit of math instruction for children aged 3-8. The course was delivered by a learning app, Zebra Al, where an intelligent tutoring system was applied. Students were invited from social networking sites and 66 children from India agreed to participate. A four-week course (five lessons each week) was delivered, covering basic math concepts including recognizing patterns, identifying 2D shapes, dissecting 2D shapes, and counting. The effect of the course was assessed in both cognitive and attitudinal facets. The results indicated that the course was effective in improving math performance and sustaining math attitudes.

keyword_papers.title: Context-sensitive Natural Language Generation for robot-assisted second language tutoring
keyword_papers.abstract: This paper describes the L2TOR intelligent tutoring system (ITS), focusing primarily on its output generation module. The L2TOR ITS is developed for the purpose of investigating the efficacy of robot-assisted second language tutoring in early childhood. We explain the process of generating contextually-relevant utterances, such as task-specific feedback messages, and discuss challenges regarding multimodality and multilingualism for situated natural language generation from a robot tutoring perspective.
